summary.text: Take the composite squarefree number \(N=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341=23492890653051\). Multiplicativity of the gcd-sum \(P\), together with \(P(p)=2p-1\) for primes, gives \(P(N)=610815156979325=26N-1\), so \(N\mid 1+P(N)\) and hence \(a(N)=1\) despite \(N\) being composite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n).
\]
Thus the sequence in the conjecture is
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+P(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite positive integer \(N\) for which \(N\mid 1+P(N)\). For such an \(N\), one has \(\gcd(N,1+P(N))=N\), and hence \(a(N)=1\). This will contradict the proposed characterization.

We first establish the facts about the gcd-sum that will be used to evaluate it.

For every positive integer \(n\),
\[
P(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d),                                      \tag{1}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. Indeed, group the integers \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq n\) according to the value \(d=\gcd(k,n)\). Such a value \(d\) must divide \(n\). If \(d\mid n\), write \(k=dj\). The condition \(\gcd(k,n)=d\) is then equivalent to
\[
1\leq j\leq n/d \quad\text{and}\quad \gcd(j,n/d)=1.
\]
There are exactly \(\varphi(n/d)\) such integers \(j\), and each corresponding summand \(\gcd(k,n)\) equals \(d\). Summing over all divisors \(d\) gives (1).

The function \(P\) is multiplicative on coprime positive integers: if \(\gcd(m,n)=1\), then
\[
P(mn)=P(m)P(n).                                                            \tag{2}
\]
To see this directly from (1), every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique form \(ef\), with \(e\mid m\) and \(f\mid n\). Moreover, all factors coming from \(m\) are coprime to all factors coming from \(n\), so
\[
\varphi\!\left(\frac{mn}{ef}\right)
 =\varphi\!\left(\frac m e\right)\varphi\!\left(\frac n f\right).
\]
Here we use the standard multiplicativity of the totient: for coprime \(r,s\), reduction modulo \(r\) and modulo \(s\) gives, by the Chinese remainder theorem, a bijection between invertible residue classes modulo \(rs\) and pairs of invertible residue classes modulo \(r\) and \(s\), so \(\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(mn)
 &=\sum_{e\mid m}\sum_{f\mid n}ef\,
   \varphi\!\left(\frac m e\right)\varphi\!\left(\frac n f\right)\\
 &=\left(\sum_{e\mid m}e\varphi(m/e)\right)
   \left(\sum_{f\mid n}f\varphi(n/f)\right)\\
 &=P(m)P(n),
\end{aligned}
\]
as claimed.

In particular, if \(p\) is prime, its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Formula (1) therefore gives
\[
P(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1.                                 \tag{3}
\]

Now consider the five integers
\[
3,\qquad 37,\qquad 43,\qquad 42307,\qquad 116341.
\]
They are distinct primes. For completeness, primality of the two larger numbers, as well as of the smaller ones, can be established by the following elementary finite certificates.

We use this criterion. Suppose \(n>1\), and the complete prime factorization of \(n-1\) is known. If, for every distinct prime \(q\mid n-1\), there is an integer \(b_q\) such that
\[
b_q^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd\bigl(b_q^{(n-1)/q}-1,n\bigr)=1,                                      \tag{4}
\]
then \(n\) is prime. To prove the criterion, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(n\), and let \(q^e\) be the exact power of \(q\) dividing \(n-1\). The first congruence in (4) implies that the multiplicative order of \(b_q\) modulo \(r\) divides \(n-1\). If that order were not divisible by \(q^e\), it would divide \((n-1)/q\), which would imply
\(r\mid b_q^{(n-1)/q}-1\). Since \(r\mid n\), this would contradict the gcd condition in (4). Thus \(q^e\mid r-1\), because an order modulo the prime \(r\) divides \(r-1\). Doing this for every prime power in \(n-1\) shows that \(n-1\mid r-1\). Hence \(r\geq n\). But \(r\mid n\) also gives \(r\leq n\), so \(r=n\). Therefore \(n\) itself is prime.

The required factorizations are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
n&n-1\\ \hline
37&2^2\cdot3^2\\
43&2\cdot3\cdot7\\
42307&2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641\\
116341&2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\end{array}
\]
The primes appearing on the right are elementary: in particular, \(277\) has no divisor among the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), which are all the primes at most \(\sqrt{277}\), and \(641\) has no divisor among \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\), which are all the primes at most \(\sqrt{641}\). Thus \(277\) and \(641\) are prime; the primality of \(2,3,5,7,11\) is immediate.

Repeated squaring modulo \(n\), followed by the Euclidean algorithm for the gcds, gives the following certificate data. In every row, the full power \(b^{n-1}\) has residue \(1\) modulo \(n\); the displayed number \(x\) is the residue of \(b^{(n-1)/q}\) modulo \(n\), and the last entry states that \(\gcd(x-1,n)=1\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r}
n&q&b&x=b^{(n-1)/q}\bmod n&\gcd(x-1,n)\\ \hline
37&2&2&36&1\\
37&3&2&26&1\\ \hline
43&2&2&42&1\\
43&3&3&36&1\\
43&7&2&21&1\\ \hline
42307&2&2&42306&1\\
42307&3&3&36715&1\\
42307&11&2&35811&1\\
42307&641&2&2666&1\\ \hline
116341&2&2&116340&1\\
116341&3&3&65539&1\\
116341&5&2&113165&1\\
116341&7&2&61355&1\\
116341&277&2&40195&1
\end{array}
\]
These data satisfy (4) for every prime divisor of each listed \(n-1\), so the criterion proves that \(37,43,42307,116341\) are prime. The number \(3\) is plainly prime as well. This finite modular computation is included only to establish rigorously that the factors used below are primes.

Define
\[
N=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341.
\]
Since these are distinct primes, the factors are pairwise coprime. Repeated use of (2), followed by (3), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(N)
 &=P(3)P(37)P(43)P(42307)P(116341)\\
 &=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
   (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
 &=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The relevant exact products are
\[
N=23492890653051

after multiplying the five prime factors, and
\[
P(N)=610815156979325.
\]
Indeed, one may track the products successively as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
\text{factors included}&\text{product of the primes}&
\text{product of the corresponding }(2p-1)\\ \hline
3&3&5\\
3,37&111&365\\
3,37,43&4773&31025\\
3,37,43,42307&201931311&2625118325\\
3,37,43,42307,116341&23492890653051&610815156979325.
\end{array}
\]
Finally,
\[
1+P(N)=610815156979326
       =26\cdot23492890653051
       =26N.                                                               \tag{5}
\]
Thus \(N\mid1+P(N)\). Equation (5) implies
\[
\gcd(N,1+P(N))=\gcd(N,26N)=N,
\]
and therefore
\[
a(N)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,1+P(N))}=\frac NN=1.
\]

On the other hand, \(N\neq1\), and \(N\) is not prime: it is divisible by \(3\), with
\(1<3<N\) (indeed, its displayed factorization has five factors greater than \(1\)). Hence for this \(N\), the assertion \(a(N)=1\) is true while the assertion “\(N=1\) or \(N\) is prime” is false.

Therefore the conjecture that, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime is false.
